# Linking people with `rLink()` {#sec-rlink}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
source("_people.R")
```

@sec-uc-link introduces `rLink()` alongside the rest of the linkage
toolbox. This chapter is about `rLink()` itself, worked from the simplest
call that does anything useful up to a staged production linkage, on the
one problem the function was written for: deciding which records are the
same **person**.

Person linkage has a shape of its own. The fields are a name --- split
into first, middle and last in one system and not split at all in the
next --- a date of birth, an address, a postcode, a phone number, an
email address and a sex or gender code. Each of them fails in its own
way, and the whole craft of the thing is knowing which failure you are
looking at:

| Field | How it goes wrong | What that means for the link |
|---|---|---|
| Surname | Marriage, hyphenation, lost apostrophes, transliteration, typing | Common, and *not* random: a disagreement is weak evidence against |
| Given name | Nicknames, initials, order swapped with the middle name | Same; `ROBERT`/`BOB` is not a typing error |
| Middle name | Simply not collected, or collapsed into the given-name field | Missing far more often than wrong |
| Date of birth | Day/month transposed, a year out, `1 January` placeholders | Strong evidence, but the placeholders will ruin a block |
| Address | People move. Abbreviations, unit prefixes, free-text additions | Agreement is strong; disagreement says almost nothing |
| Postcode | Leading zeros lost to a numeric column | A cheap, high-value blocking key once it is zero-padded |
| Phone | Shared by a household, re-used, reformatted, stale | Agreement is very strong, disagreement very weak |
| Email | Keeps a maiden name for years; case and whitespace | The same: agreement is near-proof, absence is routine |
| Sex / gender | `M`/`F`/`U` against `Male`/`Female`/`Unknown`/blank | Nearly free, and useful mostly as a *filter* |

The recurring lesson is in the last column. For a near-identifier ---
phone, email, address --- **agreement and disagreement are not mirror
images**, and a missing value is a third thing again, not a
disagreement. Most of the advanced material below is about building
comparisons that respect that.

## The smallest useful call {#sec-rlink-basic}

Two tiny files: five people in one, and four of the same five, recorded
differently, in the other.

```{r}
#| label: basic-data
hospital <- data.frame(
    frame_id   = c("HOS-01", "HOS-02", "HOS-03", "HOS-04", "HOS-05"),
    first_name = c("MARGARET", "ROBERT", "THI MINH", "WILLIAM", "ELENI"),
    last_name  = c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH", "NGUYEN", "WILLIAMS", "PAPADOPOULOS"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1948-11-02", "1979-07-23", "1962-03-14",
                           "1990-06-08", "1955-01-30")),
    postcode   = c("3121", "4000", "4032", "3065", "3181")
)
registry <- data.frame(
    frame_id   = c("REG-A", "REG-B", "REG-C", "REG-D"),
    first_name = c("MARGARET", "BOB", "MINH", "BILL"),
    last_name  = c("OBRIEN", "SMITH", "NGUYEN", "WILIAMS"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1948-11-02", "1979-07-23", "1962-03-14",
                           "1990-06-08")),
    postcode   = c("3121", "4000", "4032", "3065")
)
```

`rLink()` needs two things: **where to look** (`block_1`) and **what to
measure** (`compare`).

```{r}
#| label: basic-call
pairs <- rLink(
    hospital, registry,
    block_1 = list(dob),
    compare = list(last  = jaro_winkler(last_name),
                   first = jaro_winkler(first_name))
)
pairs[, c("pair_id", "last_name_1", "last_name_2",
          "first_name_1", "first_name_2", "last", "first")]
```

Four things happened that are worth naming, because everything later in
this chapter is a variation on them.

**`block_1` is where to look.** Comparing every record with every other
record is quadratic and almost all of it is wasted. Blocking on `dob`
says: only ever compare two people born on the same day. That is four
comparisons here instead of twenty.

**`compare` is what to measure.** Each element is a comparator call whose
first argument is the column to compare. The score column is named after
the list element --- `last`, `first` --- and an unnamed element falls
back to `<column>_<comparator>`.

**Both are ordinary R expressions evaluated against the data.** Nothing
was prepared beforehand. `soundex(last_name)` or `fsubstr(postcode, 1, 2)`
would have worked exactly as well as a bare column name, in either
argument.

**1 always means an exact match.** `jaro_winkler()` already returns 1 for
identical strings, but `levenshtein()` returns 0 and the RapidFuzz
`fuzz_*()` scorers return 100. `rLink()` probes each comparator and
converts, so you never have to remember which way a metric runs:

```{r}
#| label: basic-orientation
rLink(hospital, registry, block_1 = list(dob),
      compare = list(lev = levenshtein(last_name)))$lev
```

What it decided is recorded on the result, and is worth reading once per
project:

```{r}
#| label: basic-compare-attr
attr(pairs, "compare")
```

### Deduplicating one file

With one data frame and no second, `rLink()` finds the duplicates inside
it: pairs come back with `index_1 < index_2`, and no record is paired
with itself.

```{r}
#| label: basic-dedupe
intake <- data.frame(
    first_name = c("JENNIFER", "JEN", "DAVID", "DAVE", "PRIYA"),
    last_name  = c("TAYLOR", "TAYLOR", "ANDERSON", "ANDERSEN", "PATEL"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1971-09-19", "1971-09-19", "1964-02-29",
                           "1964-02-29", "1993-04-27"))
)
rLink(intake, block_1 = list(dob),
      compare = list(last = jaro_winkler(last_name)))[
          , c("index_1", "index_2", "last_name_1", "last_name_2", "last")]
```

## Blocking, properly {#sec-rlink-blocking}

Blocking decides what the run costs and what it is *able* to find. A
true pair that no pass puts in the same block can never be recovered, no
matter how good the comparators are. It is where a linkage usually goes
wrong, so `rLink()` makes it inspectable.

From here on the two files are the full ones from
`docs/_people.R`: an enrolment extract and a claims extract holding the
same people, recorded by two systems that agree about nothing except who
the people are.

```{r}
#| label: files
files  <- people_files(n_enrol = 20000, overlap = 0.6)
enrol  <- files$enrol
claims <- files$claims

str(enrol[1:2, ], vec.len = 2)
claims[1:3, ]
```

The claims file needs standardising before anything can be compared with
it --- the name is one `"SURNAME, Title Given Middle"` field, the date of
birth is `"DD/MM/YYYY"` text, the postcode is numeric so `0823` arrived
as `823`. @sec-uc-link does this field by field; here it is in one block.

```{r}
#| label: standardise
titles        <- c("MR", "MRS", "MS", "MISS", "DR", "PROF")
street_abbrev <- c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "CT", "PL", "TCE", "PDE", "CRES", "DR", "LN")
street_full   <- c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "COURT", "PLACE", "TERRACE",
                   "PARADE", "CRESCENT", "DRIVE", "LANE")

name <- fsquish(fupper(claims$patient_name))
rest <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 2)),
                                titles, rep("", length(titles))))
addr <- fgsub("^U[0-9]+/", "", fupper(claims$address_line))

claims_std <- data.frame(
    claim_id       = claims$claim_id,
    given_name     = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 1),
    middle_name    = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 2),
    surname        = ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 1)),
    dob            = fas.Date(claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    sex            = c(Male = "M", Female = "F", Unknown = "U")[claims$gender],
    street_address = fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(addr, ",", 1)),
                                             street_abbrev, street_full)),
    suburb         = ftrimws(fgsub(" VIC$", "", fsplit_field(addr, ",", 2))),
    postcode       = fpad(as.character(claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    phone          = claims$contact_phone,
    email          = claims$contact_email,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
claims_std$sex[is.na(claims_std$sex)] <- "U"

enrol$street_address <- fsquish(paste(enrol$number, enrol$street,
                                      enrol$street_type))
head(claims_std, 3)
```

### Check the blocking before you run it

`dry_run = TRUE` builds every key, checks every argument, and stops
without generating a single pair. On real files this takes about as long
as reading them, which means a blocking design can be argued about before
anyone waits an hour for it.

```{r}
#| label: dry-run
plan <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(
        surname_dob   = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year  = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob     = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                             postcode)
    ),
    dry_run = TRUE
)
plan
```

Two columns in that report earn their keep immediately.

`n_expected` is what each pass would cost. Summed over passes it is an
upper bound, because a pair two passes both find is counted twice ---
but it is the number that tells you whether a design is affordable.

`largest` names the five keys per pass that generate the most pairs. A
placeholder sitting at the top of that table --- `"UNKNOWN"`, `"0000"`,
a `1 January` date --- is a key that half the file shares, and it belongs
in `na_strings` or behind a `max_block_size`, not in a block.

```{r}
#| label: dry-run-largest
head(plan$largest, 6)
```

`max_pairs` is the same check, made automatically. A run expected to
exceed it stops before generating anything, naming the pass and the block
responsible:

```{r}
#| label: max-pairs
#| error: true
rLink(enrol, claims_std, block_1 = list(sex), max_pairs = 1e6)
```

### Several passes, and why

A pair is a candidate if it agrees on the key of **any one** pass. Each
pair is reported once, and `pass` records the first pass that found it.
Inside a pass, `list()` joins terms into one key, so
`list(soundex(surname), dob)` requires the same surname code **and** the
same date of birth.

That structure is how you cover the error modes one at a time. The design
above reads:

- `surname_dob` --- the workhorse. Survives spelling, not a wrong date.
- `surname_year` --- survives a transposed day and month, which the first
  pass cannot. This is the expensive one.
- `given_dob` --- survives a *married surname*, where the registered name
  is gone entirely and no amount of string comparison will find it.
- `name_postcode` --- survives a wrong date of birth, as long as they
  have not moved.

No single key could do any two of those. That is what multiple passes are
for, and the whole art is adding the pass that covers an error you can
show exists, not the pass that feels thorough.

Because these files come with a known truth, each pass can be audited:

```{r}
#| label: run-and-audit
cand <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(
        surname_dob   = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year  = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob     = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                             postcode)
    ),
    compare = list(
        surname  = jaro_winkler(surname),
        given    = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
        dob      = date_compare(dob),
        address  = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
        postcode = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(postcode)
    ),
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
    keep = c("given_name", "surname", "dob", "sex", "street_address",
             "postcode", "phone", "email")
)

truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
cbind(candidates = table(pass = cand$pass),
      true_pairs = tapply(truth, cand$pass, sum),
      yield      = round(tapply(truth, cand$pass, mean), 3))

c(true_pairs_in_data = true_pair_count(files),
  found_by_blocking  = sum(truth),
  pairs_compared     = nrow(cand),
  pairs_possible     = as.numeric(nrow(enrol)) * nrow(claims_std))
```

Read that table as a cost sheet. `surname_dob` is almost pure signal: it
finds nearly every match at a yield around 0.99. `surname_year` is the
opposite --- roughly two thirds of all the candidates, at a yield of
about 0.03 --- because dropping the day and month from the key makes the
blocks fifty times bigger. It is still worth having: it is the only pass
that survives a transposed date of birth, and the few hundred pairs it
alone contributes are exactly the ones the other three cannot reach. But
it is the first pass to tighten if the run gets too big, and the one to
point at when someone asks where the time went.

### Missing keys never pair

A record whose key is missing pairs with nothing. That is what makes it
safe to block on an incomplete field: the records with no date of birth
simply do not appear in the passes that use it, rather than colliding
into one enormous block of `NA`.

With the default `match_missing = FALSE`, a missing value in *any* term
makes the whole key for that pass missing. `na_strings` lists the text
that counts as missing --- `""` by default, which is what makes the
blank phone numbers in the claims file behave like absences rather than
like a value everybody shares.

```{r}
#| label: match-missing
a <- data.frame(surname = c("SMITH", NA, "JONES"))
b <- data.frame(surname = c("SMITH", NA))
c(default = nrow(rLink(a, b, block_1 = list(surname))),
  match_missing = nrow(rLink(a, b, block_1 = list(surname),
                             match_missing = TRUE)))
```

`match_missing = TRUE` treats "missing" as a value in its own right. It
is occasionally what you want, and almost never what you want on a
near-identifier: two people with no recorded phone number have nothing in
common.

### `block_2`, when the files disagree about shape

`block_2` gives the second file its own expressions, pass for pass, for
when the same information is stored differently:

```{r}
#| label: block-2
raw <- claims
raw$dob_text <- raw$date_of_birth               # "DD/MM/YYYY"
raw$surname_raw <- ftrimws(fsplit_field(fsquish(fupper(raw$patient_name)),
                                        ",", 1))

head(rLink(enrol, raw,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format(dob, "%d/%m/%Y"))),
           block_2 = list(list(soundex(surname_raw), dob_text)),
           compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname | surname_raw)),
           keep    = c("surname", "surname_raw"))[, -1], 3)
```

`surname | surname_raw` is the same idea in `compare`: the left of the
`|` is evaluated against `data_1`, the right against `data_2`. Either
side can be any expression, so `soundex(family_name) | surname_code`
works too. Such an element has no single column to name itself after, so
it must be given a name.

### The sorted neighbourhood, for keys that differ at the end

An exact key cannot put `SMITH` and `SMITHE` together.
`block_method = "sorted_neighbourhood"` sorts the distinct keys and pairs
records within `(window - 1) / 2` places of each other as well as those
with equal keys. Methods are set per pass, so a strict pass and a
forgiving one run in the same call:

```{r}
#| label: sn
mixed <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1      = list(strict = list(soundex(surname), dob),
                        near   = surname),
    block_method = c("exact", "sorted_neighbourhood"),
    window       = 3,
    compare      = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
    keep         = character()
)
attr(mixed, "blocking")$passes[, c("label", "method", "n_expected", "n_pairs")]
```

The window also pairs unrelated alphabetical neighbours, by design. It
belongs in a pass whose candidates are then scored, never on its own.

## Comparing person fields {#sec-rlink-compare}

Any function of two character vectors is a comparator, so the choice of
metric is a one-word edit. What matters is matching the metric to the way
the field fails.

### Names

A surname is a short string with substitutions and omissions:
`jaro_winkler()` is the standard, and `editex()` costs phonetic
substitutions (`PH`/`F`, `C`/`K`) less. A given-name field that may hold
a middle name, an initial, or the words in another order is a *token*
problem, not an edit-distance one:

```{r}
#| label: name-metrics
a <- c("JOHN PAUL", "MARY JANE", "ROBERT", "LI WEI")
b <- c("PAUL JOHN", "MARY J", "BOB", "WEI LI")
data.frame(a, b,
           jaro_winkler = round(jaro_winkler(a, b), 3),
           tokens       = round(jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b), 3),
           monge_elkan  = round(monge_elkan(a, b), 3))
```

The token comparators win decisively where the *words* moved
(`JOHN PAUL`/`PAUL JOHN`, `LI WEI`/`WEI LI`), which is the failure plain
Jaro-Winkler cannot see at all --- 0.407 for two identical names in the
other order. Where a word is merely abbreviated (`MARY JANE`/`MARY J`)
plain Jaro-Winkler does fine, and the tokens buy nothing. Pick the
comparator for the error you have.

No string metric recovers `ROBERT`/`BOB`: all three score it 0.5, and
they are right to --- the strings really are that different. Nicknames
are a lookup problem, and `freplace_tokens()` against a nickname table
*before* linking is worth more than any comparator choice.

**First / middle / last against given / last.** Two systems often split
names differently, and the usual mistake is to compare the fields that
happen to share a name. Compare the *information* instead: build one
comparable field on each side with `|`.

```{r}
#| label: name-shapes
# enrol has given / middle / surname; this extract has only given / surname,
# with the middle name folded into the given-name field where it was known.
folded <- claims_std
folded$given_all <- fsquish(paste(folded$given_name,
                                  ifelse(is.na(folded$middle_name), "",
                                         folded$middle_name)))

head(rLink(
    enrol, folded,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
    compare = list(
        surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
        # left of `|` is evaluated against enrol, right against folded
        given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(
            fsquish(paste(given_name, ifelse(is.na(middle_name), "",
                                             middle_name))) | given_all)
    ),
    keep = character())[, c("pair_id", "surname", "given")], 4)
```

### Dates of birth

A string comparator is handed text whatever the column holds, which is
what makes `jaro_winkler(dob)` work on a `Date` at all. But a date is not
a string: 1 January and 2 January are one day apart, not two characters
apart. `date_compare()` is handed the column as it is stored:

```{r}
#| label: date-compare
d1 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-14", "1985-03-14", "1985-03-14"))
d2 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-15", "1985-04-14", "1986-03-14"))
data.frame(d1, d2,
           string = round(jaro_winkler(as.character(d1), as.character(d2)), 3),
           dates  = round(date_compare(d1, d2), 3))
```

A transposed day and month is a different error again, and it is worth
its own flag rather than a tolerance --- `14/03` against `03/14` is six
months apart, which no distance will forgive:

```{r}
#| label: dob-transposed
transposed <- function(a, b) {
    pa <- date_parts(a); pb <- date_parts(b)
    as.numeric(pa$year == pb$year & pa$day == pb$month &
               pa$month == pb$day & pa$day != pa$month)
}
swapped <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
                 block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
                 compare = list(dob  = date_compare(dob),
                                swap = transposed(I(dob)),
                                sn   = jaro_winkler(surname)),
                 keep = character())
sum(swapped$swap == 1)
```

`I()` is what asks for the column as it is stored rather than as text.
`numeric_compare()` and `date_compare()` do it for you; a comparator of
your own asks for it explicitly.

### Near-identifiers: phone, email, address

Here is the point this chapter keeps returning to. For a phone number,
agreement is near-proof and disagreement is almost no evidence at all,
because people change numbers and households share them. Scoring one with
`jaro_winkler()` is actively harmful: it produces a confident-looking 0.6
for two completely different numbers.

Build the comparison to say the three things that can actually be true
--- *agrees*, *disagrees*, *not known* --- and let the missing value stay
missing:

```{r}
#| label: near-identifier
# Compare digits only, so "0412 345 678", "0412345678" and "+61 412 345 678"
# are the same number; NA where either side is blank, which is not the same
# fact as a disagreement.
same_phone <- function(a, b) {
    da <- fgsub("[^0-9]", "", a); db <- fgsub("[^0-9]", "", b)
    da <- fgsub("^61", "0", da);  db <- fgsub("^61", "0", db)
    out <- as.numeric(da == db)
    out[!nzchar(da) | !nzchar(db) | is.na(da) | is.na(db)] <- NA_real_
    out
}
same_email <- function(a, b) {
    la <- flower(ftrimws(a)); lb <- flower(ftrimws(b))
    out <- as.numeric(la == lb)
    out[!nzchar(la) | !nzchar(lb) | is.na(la) | is.na(lb)] <- NA_real_
    out
}

contact <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
    compare = list(sn    = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   phone = same_phone(phone),
                   email = same_email(email)),
    keep = character()
)
sapply(contact[, c("phone", "email")],
       function(v) c(agree = sum(v == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     disagree = sum(v == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
                     not_known = sum(is.na(v))))
```

Most pairs cannot be judged on contact details at all, which is exactly
why a *missing* score must not be collapsed into a zero. The pairs where
the phone or the email does agree, though, are as close to certain as
this kind of work gets:

```{r}
#| label: near-identifier-worth
truth_c <- same_person(files, contact$index_1, contact$index_2)
round(c(
    phone_agrees = mean(truth_c[which(contact$phone == 1)]),
    email_agrees = mean(truth_c[which(contact$email == 1)]),
    phone_differs = mean(truth_c[which(contact$phone == 0)]),
    overall = mean(truth_c)), 3)
```

A pair whose phone numbers agree is a match essentially always, and one
whose emails agree very nearly so --- against a base rate of about a
third. That is an enormous amount of evidence from a field most people
never think to compare, and it costs one exact test.

Be careful reading the other direction, though. Disagreement looks
informative here (7.5% against a 32% base rate) partly because this
simulator only reassigns a number for one matched person in eight. Real
contact data goes stale faster, and real households share landlines, so
on a live file the gap between *disagrees* and *not known* is narrower
than this. The safe design is the one above either way: score agreement,
and let non-agreement be `NA` rather than a confident zero.

An address behaves the same way, with the extra wrinkle that it is
multi-word and abbreviated, so it wants a token comparator rather than an
exact test. Sex is the cheapest field of all, and it is most useful not
as a score but as a condition --- see `filter`, below.

### Everything else

`numeric_compare()` for ages and amounts, `compare_levels()` to cut a
continuous score into agreement levels for a Fellegi-Sunter model, and
any function of your own:

```{r}
#| label: other-compare
enrol_a  <- cbind(enrol, age = as.numeric(Sys.Date() - enrol$dob) / 365.25)
claims_a <- cbind(claims_std,
                  age = as.numeric(Sys.Date() - claims_std$dob) / 365.25)
head(rLink(enrol_a, claims_a,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
           compare = list(age   = numeric_compare(age, scale = 2),
                          years = (function(a, b) abs(a - b))(I(age))),
           keep = character())[, c("age", "years")], 4)
```

A distance with no upper bound, like `years`, cannot be put on a 0--1
scale; it is returned as it is and recorded as lower-is-a-match, and
every later step reads that off `attr(x, "compare")`.

## Filtering while scoring {#sec-rlink-filter}

Blocking is deliberately generous, so most candidates are not matches and
get thrown away the moment they are scored. `filter` does the throwing
away *inside* `rLink()`:

```{r}
#| label: filter
kept <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.85 & gn >= 0.80 & (sex_1 == sex_2 | sex_1 == "U" | sex_2 == "U"),
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
    keep    = c("surname", "given_name", "sex")
)
unlist(attr(kept, "filter")[c("n_candidates", "n_scored", "n_kept")])
```

The rule is an ordinary R expression giving `TRUE` for the pairs to keep.
It can name any score, `pass`, and any column of either input under its
suffix. Three properties make it more than a convenience:

**Conditions that read no score are applied first.** The `sex` clause
above needs no comparator, so it runs before scoring and the comparators
never see the pairs it drops. The order you write the conditions in makes
no difference; the result is identical to scoring everything and
subsetting.

**The expensive columns are built only for survivors.** `pair_id` above
all --- R takes about a second to make a million new strings, whoever
asks it to --- and then the carried columns.

**The 2^31 candidate-pair ceiling goes away.** Pairs are generated,
scored and thinned a slice at a time, so the full candidate set never
exists at once; only the pairs kept have to fit in one table.

A rule that mentions no score needs no `compare` at all, which makes
`filter` a way to express a candidate condition that no blocking key
could:

```{r}
#| label: filter-no-compare
nrow(rLink(enrol, claims_std,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1))),
           filter  = abs(as.numeric(dob_1 - dob_2)) <= 31,
           keep    = character()))
```

## Identifying pairs, so a judgement survives {#sec-rlink-pairid}

`pair_id` identifies each pair. By default it is `"<id_1>|<id_2>"` built
from the `frame_id` column of each input, and it falls back to numbering
the pairs when either input has no such column. Two different names are
given as `pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id")`.

This matters more than it looks. An identifier built from the records is
**stable**: the same two records give the same `pair_id` whatever
blocking found them. A row number is not.

```{r}
#| label: pair-id
run_a <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character())
run_b <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), dob)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character())
c(run_a = nrow(run_a), run_b = nrow(run_b),
  same_pairs = length(intersect(run_a$pair_id, run_b$pair_id)))
```

Every clerical judgement recorded in @sec-rlink-inspect is filed against
this column, which is the only reason those judgements still apply after
the blocking is changed and the linkage re-run. An identifier containing
`"|"` is an error rather than an ambiguous key, and missing or repeated
identifiers raise a warning saying how many.

Building it is the slowest thing `rLink()` does on a large result.
`filter` avoids it for the pairs it drops; `pair_id = NULL` avoids it
altogether, for a run whose pairs will be thresholded and clustered but
never reviewed. `attr(x, "timings")` reports it as its own stage:

```{r}
#| label: timings
attr(cand, "timings")
```

## Deciding, and what comes after {#sec-rlink-decide}

`rLink()` stops at scored pairs. Turning those into links is a separate
decision, and the package gives you three ways to make it.

### Hand weights

Defensible when the fields are few and the project can justify the
numbers:

```{r}
#| label: hand-weights
cand$score <- with(cand,
    (3 * surname + 2 * given + 2 * dob + address + postcode) / 9)
truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
qs <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
round(rbind(same_person = quantile(cand$score[truth], qs),
            different   = quantile(cand$score[!truth], qs)), 3)
```

### A Fellegi-Sunter model

`rLink_weights()` estimates how much each field's agreement is actually
worth, by EM, from the candidate pairs themselves --- no truth set
needed. It replaces the guesswork above with a `weight` in bits and a
`probability`, and it can adjust for term frequency so that agreeing on a
rare surname counts for more than agreeing on `SMITH`.

```{r}
#| label: weights
scored <- rLink_weights(cand, tf = "surname")
head(scored[order(-weight),
            c("surname", "given", "dob", "weight", "probability")], 4)
attr(scored, "model")$fit
```

```{r}
#| label: weights-check
round(c(
    precision_at_0.9 = mean(truth[scored$probability > 0.9]),
    recall_at_0.9    = sum(truth & scored$probability > 0.9) /
                       true_pair_count(files)), 4)
```

### What a cut-off would do, without a truth set

`threshold_sweep()` reports, for each candidate cut-off, how many pairs
survive, how many are cleanly one-to-one, and how many records end up
contested --- which is the signal you have when nobody knows the answer.

```{r}
#| label: sweep
threshold_sweep(scored, "probability",
                thresholds = c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999))[
    , c("threshold", "n_pairs", "n_one_to_one", "n_conflict_1", "n_conflict_2")]
```

### One-to-one resolution, and entities

If each person can appear at most once in each file, say so.
`select_greedy()` keeps each record's best partner and drops the rest,
which removes most of the chaining risk before clustering:

```{r}
#| label: greedy
links <- scored[scored$probability > 0.9]
best  <- select_greedy(links$index_1, links$index_2, links$weight)
c(accepted = nrow(links), one_to_one = sum(best),
  precision = round(mean(truth[scored$probability > 0.9][best]), 4))
```

```{r}
#| label: cluster
one <- links[best]
entity <- cluster_pairs(one$index_1, one$index_2 + nrow(enrol),
                        n = nrow(enrol) + nrow(claims_std))
table(cluster_size = tabulate(entity))
```

## Staged linkage {#sec-rlink-staged}

A large linkage is rarely one run. The usual shape is a strict pass whose
links nobody needs to look at, then a looser pass over what is left, and
two arguments keep the second from repeating the first.

**`exclude`** names pairs to leave out. They are dropped as soon as they
are found, before scoring, so pairs already settled cost nothing the
second time. Given as a character vector they are read as `pair_id`s and
found again through the identifier columns --- which is what makes them
safe to carry between runs, since the files may have been re-ordered,
added to or cut down in between.

**`rLink_unmatched()`** is the other half: the records that no accepted
link reaches, which are the ones a second run is for.

```{r}
#| label: staged
# Stage 1: strict. Same surname code and full date of birth, names close.
stage1 <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.95 & gn >= 0.90,
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character()
)

# Stage 2: looser, over the records stage 1 did not reach, and explicitly
# not re-examining anything stage 1 already settled.
left_1 <- rLink_unmatched(stage1, side = 1, n = nrow(enrol))
left_2 <- rLink_unmatched(stage1, side = 2, n = nrow(claims_std))

stage2 <- rLink(
    enrol[left_1, ], claims_std[left_2, ],
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), dob),
                   list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                   ad = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.80 | ad >= 0.90,
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character()
)

c(stage1_links = nrow(stage1),
  enrol_left = length(left_1), claims_left = length(left_2),
  stage2_candidates = nrow(stage2))
```

```{r}
#| label: staged-precision
round(c(
    stage1_precision = mean(same_person(files, stage1$index_1, stage1$index_2)),
    stage1_recall    = sum(same_person(files, stage1$index_1,
                                       stage1$index_2)) /
                       true_pair_count(files)), 4)
```

Stage 1 is perfectly precise on this data, and that is the point: those
links never need a human. Stage 2 is where the judgement is, and
@sec-rlink-inspect is about making that judgement recordable.

One trap in that code. Stage 2 was run on *subsets*, so its `index_1`
and `index_2` are positions in `enrol[left_1, ]` and
`claims_std[left_2, ]`, not in the original files --- `left_1[index_1]`
converts them back. This is precisely why a stable `pair_id` is worth
having: it means the same thing in both stages, so the two results stack
without any index arithmetic at all.

The same two arguments also express "re-run with better blocking, but do
not ask me about the pairs I have already ruled on":

```{r}
#| label: exclude
again <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
               exclude = stage1$pair_id,
               keep    = character())
unlist(attr(again, "exclude"))
```

## Candidates from somewhere else {#sec-rlink-pairs}

`pairs` scores candidates found any other way, instead of blocking: any
data frame with `x_index` and `y_index`, which is the shape
`minhash_pairs()`, `fuzzy_within()` and `tfidf_top_n()` all return. It is
the escape hatch for when no key is good enough --- long free-text
addresses, organisation names, anything where the useful signal is spread
across the whole string.

```{r}
#| label: pairs-arg
near <- tfidf_top_n(claims_std$street_address[1:200],
                    enrol$street_address, top_n = 2)
head(rLink(enrol, claims_std[1:200, ],
           pairs   = data.frame(x_index = near$table_index,
                                y_index = near$query_index),
           compare = list(ad = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
                          sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
           keep    = "street_address")[, -1], 4)
```

## At scale

The whole thing on ten times the data, with `keep = character()` so that
nothing but the indices and the scores is carried:

```{r}
#| label: scale
big <- people_files(n_enrol = 200000, overlap = 0.6)
nm <- fsquish(fupper(big$claims$patient_name))
rs <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 2)),
                              titles, rep("", length(titles))))
big_std <- data.frame(
    given_name = fsplit_field(rs, " ", 1),
    surname    = ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 1)),
    dob        = fas.Date(big$claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    postcode   = fpad(as.character(big$claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

system.time(
    out <- rLink(big$enrol, big_std,
        block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob),
                       list(soundex(given_name), dob),
                       list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                            postcode)),
        compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                       given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                       dob     = date_compare(dob)),
        keep = character())
)
c(records_1 = nrow(big$enrol), records_2 = nrow(big_std),
  pairs_possible = as.numeric(nrow(big$enrol)) * nrow(big_std),
  pairs_compared = nrow(out),
  blocking_recall = round(sum(same_person(big, out$index_1, out$index_2)) /
                          true_pair_count(big), 4))
```

## Argument reference

| Argument | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `data_1`, `data_2` | The inputs. One alone deduplicates. Never modified. |
| `block_1`, `block_2` | Blocking passes, as R expressions. `block_2` for when the files store it differently. |
| `compare` | Comparator calls. `NULL` returns unscored candidates. |
| `pairs` | Candidates from elsewhere, instead of `block_1`. |
| `block_method`, `window` | `"exact"` or `"sorted_neighbourhood"`, per pass. |
| `max_block_size` | Skip blocks bigger than this, with a warning and a per-pass count. |
| `match_missing`, `na_strings` | Whether missing keys pair; what counts as missing. |
| `force_upper_case` | Upper-case keys and comparison values. Never changes the columns returned. |
| `normalise` | Convert scores so 1 means an exact match. |
| `keep` | Columns to carry. `NULL` is all, `character()` is none. |
| `pair_id` | Identifier column(s) to build `pair_id` from. |
| `block_key` | Add the readable `block_key` column. `FALSE` saves one string per pair. |
| `suffixes`, `score_position` | How the output is laid out. |
| `filter` | Keep only matching pairs, cheaply, while scoring. |
| `exclude` | Pairs to leave out, by `pair_id` or by row number. |
| `dry_run`, `max_pairs` | Check the blocking without running it; stop a run that is too big. |
| `nthreads`, `verbose` | Thread cap; progress and diagnostics. |

And on the result: `attr(x, "blocking")`, `attr(x, "compare")`,
`attr(x, "timings")`, `attr(x, "filter")`, `attr(x, "exclude")`,
`attr(x, "n_records")` and `attr(x, "dedupe")`. All of them survive `[`,
`order()` and `head()`.

```{r}
#| label: summary
summary(cand)
```
